corrected_draft.title: CREW Reports Trump Visited His Properties on 191 of 512 Days
corrected_draft.description_short: CREW counted 191 days with Trump property visits in his first 512 days back in office, or 37%; the analysis does not substantiate the held entry’s $115 million cost total.
corrected_draft.description_medium: A June 16, 2026 CREW analysis said Donald Trump had visited properties he owns on 191 of his first 512 days back in office, or 37%. CREW separately counted 259 individual property visits, including 148 golf-course visits, because Trump sometimes visited more than one property in a day. The article does not report the held entry’s $115 million cumulative golf-travel cost or its $300 million projection.
corrected_draft.description_long: On June 16, 2026, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington reported that Donald Trump had visited resorts and golf courses he still profits from on 191 of the first 512 days of his second term, equal to 37% of those days. CREW also counted 259 individual property visits, including 148 visits to golf courses; that number exceeds the day count because more than one property visit can occur in a single day. The article lists 102 visits to Mar-a-Lago and says Secret Service records showed nearly $100,000 spent at Trump properties in the first few months of the second term. It notes that the amount excludes costs from other agencies and discusses Air Force One operating costs by citing a Palm Beach Post analysis. The article does not establish the held entry’s $115 million cumulative travel-and-security figure or its $300 million end-of-term projection. Those totals need a separate auditable source and methodology.

remaining_gap: CREW supports the 191-of-512-day property-visit count; the exact unsupported claim is $115 million in cumulative second-term golf travel/security cost and a $300 million end-of-term projection. corrected_draft.title: Supreme Court clears path for possible dismissal of Bannon contempt case
corrected_draft.description_short: On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the appeals court ruling upholding Steve Bannon’s contempt conviction and remanded the case.
corrected_draft.description_medium: Reuters reported that DOJ told the justices dismissal was in the interests of justice and had already filed a dismissal motion in the trial court. Bannon had been convicted in 2022 after defying a congressional subpoena and served a four-month sentence in 2024. The Supreme Court docket lists a February 9, 2026 filing by the United States.
corrected_draft.description_long: Steve Bannon was convicted in 2022 on two counts of contempt of Congress for refusing to provide documents or testimony to the House committee investigating the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. The D.C. Circuit upheld his conviction in May 2024, and the Supreme Court denied his request to remain out of prison while appealing in June 2024. Bannon served a four-month federal prison sentence later that year. On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the appellate judgment and remanded the matter. Reuters reported that DOJ told the Court dismissal was in the interests of justice and had already filed a dismissal motion in district court. The remand returned the case to the trial court for further proceedings; DOJ’s motion still required judicial action. The appellate judgment was vacated; the Supreme Court did not itself enter a dismissal. This account is limited to the procedural action and the government’s reported position.
corrected_draft.draft_limitation: Draft contains only facts directly supported by the cited sources.

remaining_gap: Confirm the remand and DOJ dismissal-motion posture against the cited Supreme Court docket and Reuters report during editorial review; no dismissal is described as completed.

child_drafts.description_long: On April 24, 2025, President Trump issued a memorandum directing the Attorney General, in consultation with the Treasury Secretary, to investigate allegations that online fundraising platforms had facilitated unlawful straw-donor or foreign contributions in U.S. elections. The memorandum specifically cited congressional findings concerning ActBlue and instructed officials to assess whether existing laws had been violated and whether further action was warranted. The action was a directive to investigate allegations; it did not itself establish that ActBlue or any other platform had violated campaign-finance law. ActBlue denied wrongdoing and characterized the action as politically motivated in contemporaneous reporting. A separate later episode concerning the Open Society Foundations is not demonstrated to be the same investigation or a continuation of this memorandum and should not be included in this event without source evidence linking them. The memorandum is a direction to examine allegations, not a finding of a campaign-finance violation.
